title: Benchmarking Methodology and Latency Distributions
objectives: Compute mean, median and tail percentiles for a latency sample and explain when each is honest
Explain why warmup is required and what cold-start costs look like
Diagnose coordinated omission in a load generator and fix it with open-loop design
Define a benchmarking discipline that makes p99 regressions visible
motivation: A benchmark that says 'mean 2 µs' can hide a 12 µs mode that fires exactly when the market moves, the only time latency matters. Low-latency engineering is a measurement discipline: percentiles over averages, warmup over cold starts, and load generators that keep sending when things get slow.

blocks.md: Latency distributions are not tidy bells; they are **mixtures**, a fast mode (cache-resident, branch-predicted) and a slow tail (cache misses, TLB misses, interrupts, page faults). The mean blends the modes into a number that *nothing ever measured*. And the tail is not cosmetic: your slowest responses cluster when the market is busiest, which is exactly when being slow costs the trade.

blocks.tex: \bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} x_i \qquad \text{vs} \qquad p_{99} = \text{the value below which } 99\% \text{ of samples fall}
blocks.caption: The mean summarises everything at once; a percentile points at the part that trades.

blocks.title: A 100-sample illustration (µs, synthetic)
items: 95 samples at 1.0 (the fast mode), 4 at 1.5, 1 at 12.0 (one page-faulted outlier).
Median (p50) $= 1.0\,\mu s$; p99 $≈ 12\,\mu s$ - more than ten times the mean.

The mean said 'fast'; the tail said 'occasionally catastrophic'. In trading terms: 99 of 100 quotes are fine, and the 1 slow one arrives after the market moved, which is the one that trades against you.

blocks.md: Report at least **p50, p90, p99, p99.9 and max**, with sample counts. Percentiles are rank statistics: solid to outlier scaling and interpretable as service levels. **Regression gates** belong on p99, not the mean, a change that improves the mean 5% while worsening p99 by 50% is a traded-tail disaster wearing a good headline. Beware small samples: p99.9 of 200 samples is essentially the worst sample you happened to record. Gather more data, or honestly report fewer nines.

blocks.text: Warmup: the first N measurements are fiction

blocks.md: Cold runs pay one-time costs that steady state never repeats: page faults mapping memory, TLB and cache fills, branch-predictor training, allocator arenas growing. A benchmark that includes them reports a mixture of 'first time' and 'every time'. Discipline: run a **warmup phase** (discard it, or record it separately), then measure a **steady-state** window. Production behaves like steady state, except at 4 a.m. restarts, which is why cold-start behaviour is measured too, just never averaged in.

blocks.text: Coordinated omission: the benchmark's blind spot

blocks.md: A **closed-loop** load generator sends the next request only after the previous response returns. Suppose response #7 hangs for 500 ms at an intended rate of 10 requests/s: about $10 \times 0.5 = 5$ requests that *should* have been sent were never issued, so their (probably terrible) latencies are missing from the histogram. The system got in trouble and the benchmark **coordinated its silence with the outage**, measurements look fine while users suffer. Fixes: run **open-loop** (send on a fixed schedule regardless of responses), or record each request's *virtual start time* and correct the intervals afterwards. Rule: a benchmark only measures the requests it dared to send.

blocks.code:
samples = [1.0] * 95 + [1.5] * 4 + [12.0]
xs = sorted(samples)
n = len(xs)
mean = sum(xs) / n
print(round(mean, 2), xs[n // 2], xs[-1])
blocks.caption: Prints: 1.13 1.0 12.0, mean, median and max for the illustration above. Three honest numbers, three different stories.

blocks.md: Benchmarking latency is measurement science, not stopwatch use. The three failure modes that invalidate most naive benchmarks, measuring the wrong thing (wall clock including setup), measuring on an uncontrollable system (CPU frequency scaling, other processes), and summarising with the wrong statistic (the mean, always the mean), all have standard defences. Learn the defences once; every measurement you take afterwards becomes trustworthy.

blocks.title: The methodology, as a checklist that fits on a sticky note
items: **Pin the environment**: performance governor set, turbo behaviour known (or disabled), the benchmark pinned to specific cores (`taskset`), background noise off. An unpinned benchmark is a weather report.

**Warm up, then measure**: cold caches and lazy page faults belong to the first iterations; discard them. Measure steady state, and separately measure the cold case only if cold is the production scenario (it usually is not).

**Collect the distribution, not the total**: every iteration is a sample of a distribution that is never normal (GC-like pauses, page faults, IRQ storms live in the tail). Save per-iteration latencies; report p50/p99/p99.9/max, never a lone mean. The PercentileExplorer lab makes the mean-vs-tail gap visceral.

**Repeat to bound noise**: run the whole benchmark $k$ times and compare the *spread of the p99s* across runs. If run-to-run p99 varies by 30%, your measurement resolution is 30%, no optimisation smaller than that is detectable, and claiming one is astrology.

**Compare like with like**: before/after on the same machine, same pinning, same warmup, and report the environment with the numbers. A latency claim without an environment description is not a result.

rows: cache misses, IPC, branch misses (hardware counters)

blocks.title: The optimisation you cannot measure, twice
blocks.md: The most expensive engineering sin in low latency: shipping an optimisation whose gain is smaller than measurement noise, it added complexity and bought nothing, and now nobody dares remove it. The sticky-note checklist exists to make your noise floor explicit so every change is either *proven* or *rejected*. That binary is the entire value of methodology.

items: Fix CPU frequency / disable deep idle on benchmark machines; pin threads (previous lessons).
Warm up; measure steady state separately from cold start.
Use open-loop load at realistic rates, including bursts; never let the generator pause under load.
Record raw distributions (histograms), not just summaries; report conditions, hardware, kernel, versions, data sizes.
Gate releases on p99/p99.9 deltas, and rerun anything suspicious, noise reproduces itself.

blocks.title: Averages in production dashboards
blocks.md: A 'mean latency 2 µs' panel hides the 14:32 spike that cost the afternoon. Instrument percentiles end-to-end (NIC to order out), alert on p99, and keep the raw histogram, you will need it for the incident review.

guidedExercise.prompt: 20 steady-state samples (µs): eighteen at 2.0, one at 2.5, one at 30.0. (a) Mean? (b) Median? (c) Max? (d) Which number would you gate a release on, and what would the mean have hidden?
hints: Median of 20 sorted samples sits between the 10th and 11th values.
guidedExercise.solution: (a) $(18 \times 2.0 + 2.5 + 30.0) / 20 = (36 + 32.5) / 20 = 68.5 / 20 = 3.425\,\mu s$. (b) Sorted, ranks 10 and 11 are both 2.0, so the median is $2.0\,\mu s$. (c) $30.0\,\mu s$. (d) Gate on the tail (max / p99): the mean of 3.425 blends one pathological 30 µs event into invisibility, exactly the event that trades against you.

independentExercise.prompt: Two builds, 100 samples each (µs). Build A: 98 samples at 2.0 and two at 6.0. Build B: 99 samples at 2.1 and one at 3.0. (a) Mean of each. (b) Approximate p99 of each (with 100 samples, p99 ≈ the 99th sorted value). (c) Which build ships, and why is 'A has the lower mean' the wrong reason?
hints: Sort each set and take the 99th value.
independentExercise.solution: (a) A: $(98 \times 2.0 + 2 \times 6.0)/100 = (196 + 12)/100 = 2.08\,\mu s$; B: $(99 \times 2.1 + 3.0)/100 = (207.9 + 3.0)/100 = 2.109\,\mu s$. (b) A's 99th sorted value is 6.0; B's is 3.0. (c) Ship **B**: the mean difference (2.109 vs 2.08) is noise, but the tail (3.0 vs 6.0) is structural, in trading, the p99 quote is the one that trades when the market moves.

commonMistakes: Reporting only the mean (or worse, best-of-N), tails are the traded risk.
Benchmarking cold: page faults and TLB misses measure the reboot, not the design.
Closed-loop generators that pause during slow responses: coordinated omission hides exactly the samples that matter.
Changing several things between runs, one variable at a time, or the delta is unattributable.
realWorldApplication: Latency-sensitive teams publish percentile SLOs and gate releases on p99 regressions; open-loop load tools and HdrHistogram-style recorder percentiles are standard kit in performance engineering.
quantFinanceApplication: A market maker's slow 1% of quotes is the 1% that trades when news hits, percentile discipline converts 'usually fast' into a defensible statement about worst-case exposure.
summary: Latency distributions are mixtures; the mean blends modes into a value nothing measured, publish p50/p90/p99/p99.9/max.
Warmup discards one-time cold costs (page faults, TLB/cache fills, predictor training); production ≈ steady state, cold starts measured separately.
Coordinated omission: closed-loop generators stop sending during slow responses, hiding the worst latency; fix with open-loop schedules or virtual start times.
Gate releases on tail percentiles with recorded conditions; a benchmark only measures the requests it dared to send.

quiz.prompt: The 100-sample illustration: 95 samples at 1.0 µs, 4 at 1.5 µs, 1 at 12.0 µs. What is the mean, in µs?

options: The average of the slowest 1% of samples
The value below which 99% of samples fall (≈1% exceed it)
A latency that occurs 99 times per second
quiz.explanation: p99 is a rank statistic on the sorted distribution, the 99th percentile, not an average of anything and not arrival order.

quiz.prompt: Open-loop arithmetic: intended rate 10 requests/s; one response takes 500 ms. How many requests should have been sent during that window (and were suppressed by a closed-loop generator)?
quiz.explanation: $10 / s \times 0.5\,s = 5$ requests, five unmeasured, probably-terrible latencies: coordinated omission.

quiz.prompt: Which belong in a sound benchmarking discipline?
options: Warm up before measuring; report steady state separately
Pin threads and fix CPU frequency
Use open-loop load generation at realistic rates
Report only the mean to keep dashboards clean
quiz.explanation: Warmup, controlled hardware and open-loop load are the discipline; mean-only reporting is precisely what hides tails.

quiz.prompt: Why must benchmarks warm up before measuring?
quiz.modelAnswer: Cold runs pay one-time costs, page faults, TLB and cache fills, branch-predictor training, that steady state never repeats; including them measures the restart, not the system under production conditions.
quiz.explanation: Warmup separates 'first time' costs from 'every time' costs so the measured distribution describes production behaviour.

flashcards.back: Mean: sum/n, blends modes into a value nothing measured. p99: value below which 99% of samples fall, the traded tail. Release gates belong on p99.
A closed-loop load generator pauses while responses are slow, so the worst latencies are never sampled. Fix: open-loop sending or virtual start-time correction.
Discard or record separately the first N runs: page faults, TLB/cache fills and predictor training are one-time costs, not steady-state behaviour.
The slow 1% of responses clusters when the market is busiest, exactly when stale quotes trade against you.
